Our inclusion of the Good-Bad IAT in addition to the American-Foreign IAT was largely exploratory. We predicted (as listed in Hypothesis 4) that the American-Foreign IAT may capture a unique source of variance in the social priming data because of a relationship specifically between the construct of foreignness and expectations about L2 accent.

[PAPER_0071, relevance_score=0.445] If this was the case, including the Good-Bad IAT would provide useful discriminant validity.

Here, we outline the overarching and experiment-specific hypotheses of the present study:

Hypothesis 1: For Experiments 1 and 2: Race/ethnicity primes (images of a White, East Asian, vs. Latina face) will affect the perception of American, L1-accented English in babble. Specifically, subjects will have better transcription accuracy for the White prime than the East Asian or the Latina prime.

[PAPER_0072, relevance_score=0.384] Hypothesis 3: For all experiments: Individual listeners' implicit associations will be related to the size of their "social priming effects" (Figure 1). The size of the difference between conditions (e.g., transcription performance for a White vs. an East Asian prime) will vary by listener, and we expect that listeners with larger priming effects will have stronger implicit associations between these races/ethnicities and the constructs American versus Foreign.

Hypothesis 4: For all experiments: The relationship between social priming costs and implicit associations will depend on the type of IAT.

[PAPER_0073, relevance_score=0.314] Specifically, we expect that the Good-Bad IAT will not significantly predict social priming costs, while the American-Foreign IAT will, confirming a unique relationship between the construct of foreignness and social priming effects.

[PAPER_0126, relevance_score=0.338] Primary Analyses

Model specifications matched those in the analysis of Experiment 1 with the exception of the random effects. Model comparisons indicated that random slopes for speaker did not improve model fit, and were thus dropped from the random effect structure. Fixed effects in the glmer() model included: prime (dummy-coded levels: Latinx, White), American-Foreign D score, Good-Bad D score, and counterbalance (dummy-coded levels: counterbalance L-W, counterbalance W-L), as well as interactions between prime and each additional predictor.

[PAPER_0137, relevance_score=0.399] Log-likelihood model comparisons are summarized in Table 7.

[From Experiment 1, cited for: Random and fixed effects in the between-subject analysis] This change required the random effect structure to be altered to include only random intercepts of subjects and items.

[From Experiment 1, cited for: Random and fixed effects in the between-subject analysis] Fixed effects for the analysis included: prime (dummy-coded levels: East Asian, White), American-Foreign D score, Good-Bad D score, and interactions between prime and these two other effects.

[PAPER_0140, relevance_score=0.341] Exploratory Analyses

Bayesian Analysis

As in Experiment 1, we conducted an exploratory analysis of the null outcome for the social priming manipulation using a Bayesian pair-wise t-test in JASP (Love et al., 2019). The predicted variable was the mean proportion of keywords correctly identified by subject for each of the prime conditions (White and Latinx). Settings selected for the Student's t-test with an alternative hypothesis of White ≠ Latinx.

[PAPER_0145, relevance_score=0.367] Random effects included intercepts by subject and by item. Only the fixed effect of prime was entered into the model, and it did not improve model fit (χ2 = 0.02, df = 1, p = .90), reaffirming the null outcomes of the primary analyses.

[PAPER_0129, relevance_score=0.255] [From Experiment 1, cited for: Primary model specifications, except random effects] That is, each trial of the task (for a given subject) corresponded to a single row of the dataframe in R (a full target sentence), and the predicted variable of the models was two columns: count of correctly identified target words and count of missed target words.6 Although there are multiple keywords per sentence/trial, the generalized linear mixed-effects regression (GLMER) model is nonetheless able to predict both the counts of the correct versus missed target words using a binomial regression.

[PAPER_0144, relevance_score=0.252] Combined Analysis of Speech Transcription Tasks Across Experiments

Based on the analyses of Block 1, it appeared that the insignificant effects of prime were, nonetheless, consistent in direction and size across experiments. Thus, we decided to examine the effect of prime within Block 1 in a combined data set using GLMER, with the levels of East Asian and Latina combined into a single level: Minority. Our aim was to increase power to detect a difference between primes (N = 689; 345 White, 344 Minority). Random effects included intercepts by subject and by item.

[PREREG_0030, relevance_score=0.222] The mean latency for correct trials is calculated for each block, and error trial latencies are replaced with these values plus an additional 600 ms. One pooled standard deviation is computed for all trials in Blocks 3 and 6, and another for all trials in Blocks 4 and 7. The average latencies for each block are used to calculate differences between Blocks 3 and 6 and between Blocks 4 and 7 (specifically, later blocks minus earlier blocks). These differences are then divided by their respective pooled standard deviations, and then averaged to obtain a final d value.

[PREREG_0031, relevance_score=0.258] Blocks 3 and 6 are paired together during this process because they contain the earlier trials of each race-attribute pairing, which typically have slower response times than Blocks 4 and 7. Both group-wide and individual d-scores will be calculated (group-wide for scoring purposes).
